Why does light take so long to escape a star? A random walk, from a 3D atmosphere to the blackboard
Play
Apparently I keep coming back to this example... The hair, shirt and classroom change a bit with the years; the random walk remains. Consistency of a physics professor, perhaps? :-)

Here we go from a photon finding its way through our 3D model atmosphere to the simplest possible blackboard model: one step forwards, or one step backwards. The average displacement is zero, so that won’t get us very far. The mean square gives us something more useful.

The neat up-and-down argument is inspired by The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, §6–3, “The random walk”. Still my favourite way to get to that familiar square root of N.

Lectures and visualisations by Jon Sundqvist, Institute of Astronomy, KU Leuven. The stellar-atmosphere calculation is part of SUPERSTARS-3D.

A note on the two examples in the opening: the 9.7 million scatterings and roughly 98 minutes describe this particular path through our simulated hot-star atmosphere. The roughly 100,000-year solar diffusion timescale refers to a different problem and depends on the solar model.

Questions and corrections are welcome, as always. Enjoy :-)

text:
Those Kepler-138s
Today I had planned on writing about Water Worlds; I picked two, Kepler-138 c and d. Their bulk density, that is their radii and mass estimates tell us there is significant water on both. Here are the rendering my own algorithm came up with.

u/Exoplanetary-Systems - Kepler-138 c, credit: author at https://exoplanetary.systems
Kepler-138 c, credit: author at https://exoplanetary.systems
u/Exoplanetary-Systems - Kepler-138 d, credit author at https://exoplanetary.systems
Kepler-138 d, credit author at https://exoplanetary.systems
Wait a sec, the astute reader might notice. Those are not water worlds, those are hot, dry scorched worlds with one side baked to lava from being tidally locked forever facing its star. Did you cut-n-paste the wrong images, perhaps?

After checking, I find my algorithm to be correct. These two worlds have orbital periods of 14 and 23 days respectively. That’s how long their year is. Their distance from their star is 0.09 and 0.12 AU. (Earth is at 1 AU from our sun.) These tell us these planets orbit unimaginably close to their star. That would make these worlds tidally locked with the same side continually facing the sun, the same way our moon is tidally locked to Earth.

Yet, this article in EarthSky, https://earthsky.org/space/water-worlds-kepler-138-c-kepler-138-d-exoplanets/ tells us these are indeed water worlds. I have no reason to dispute a well-respected publication.

This case exemplifies a broader problem: with only mass, radius, orbital period, and stellar luminosity estimates, I’m triangulating a world from four numbers. I can’t tell you if there’s an atmosphere, what it’s made of, whether the water is liquid or steam or ice, what color the sky is, whether there are continents. Every artistic choice: the cloud cover, the sea color, the terminator gradient, on any planet is an educated guess. Here is a simplified table of the data I use to update my database from Nasa’s JPL database. This is all I go on.

u/Exoplanetary-Systems - Snippet of my weekly download of exoplanets. Source from https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/TAP/sync?query=select+*+from+ps&format=json
Snippet of my weekly download of exoplanets. Source from https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/TAP/sync?query=select+*+from+ps&format=json
This gives me: the orbital period, orbital distance, the planet’s mass; radius; density; and then some data about the host star like the radius, mass, and luminosity. From the orbital distance, my formula determined these worlds to be tidally locked hot eyeball worlds. From the from density and radius data the article’s author determined them to be water-worlds. Both are correct.

The James Webb Space Telescope will one day give us actual atmospheric spectra for Kepler-138 c and d. When that happens I’ll have more data points and can make better educated guesses. I’m taken back to an earlier article of mine, “To What End?” in which Hypatia of Alexandria mapped the sky with instruments that couldn’t resolve a planet’s face. Now we’ve refined our instruments to detect molecular signatures in exoplanet atmospheres. We still can’t say with confidence what these Kepler-138 planets look like from the surface. The gap between “we detected water vapor” and “here is what the ocean looks like” is where we live. It’s a fantastic time to be alive.

Could a universe devoid of matter and energy exist?
Could a realm of totally empty space possibly exist? A place without matter, without energy, without particles or a single atom, with no singularity for anything to explode from but only a simple void, how could “existence” be determined? Obviously, this is purely a thought exercise because without an observer to recognize and identify the state of “being”, there’s no awareness to define it. Looking from the outside into what could only be described as an empty black bag of nothingness, how could such a place be measured? Is it big or small and relative to what standard with nothing in it to define any dimensions? Time would still exist if it is an intrinsic feature of “space” and inseparable from it, but what quality could define space with nothing occupying it to measure it against and no awareness to recognize it? It seems to follow that no version of “reality” is possible without, at minimum, a single partical or atom for it to contain. There can be no “container” without something for it to contain. In our universe, space isn’t “nothing” because it exists and contains all the “somethings” in our reality. It has certain features in that it can be warped by mass and its expansion can be measured relative to bits of matter moving apart to create “dimension”. Without something to compare nothing against, how could anything be? It seems therefore that for a universe to exist, it must have something in it to qualify it. But can there be any “something” without some form of awareness to acknowledge it? Otherwise, how can it be defined as “real”?

Does this mean then that matter/energy must be for a universe to exist and is therefore intrinsic to its manifestation? Wouldn't it also then follow that some kind of awareness would also be needed to define “something” vs “nothing”, thereby making consciousness an essential part of reality itself? After all, how could anything be without an observer to acknowledge that there is “something” as opposed to “nothing”? Doesn't this mean that no objective reality is possible without some awareness to acknowledge it's existence? As such, it seems both matter/energy and a consciousness to acknowledge it is not “nothing” are required for a universe to exist at all.

text:
51 Pegasi b, the Nobel Prize Exoplanet
You know the Doppler effect, when a screaming siren has a different pitch when it approaches vs. when it recedes? That’s how the exoplanet, 51 Pegasi b was discovered, and the technique is called the radial velocity method.

In 1995 two scientists, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz made the discovery that the star 51 Pegasi had a wobble, a Doppler shift. The cycle was every four days. The conclusion was that a planet orbited every four days, and to perturb the star so, it must be a giant.

The planet was named 51 Pegasi b, the b became the naming convention for objects associated with a star. B being the first, c the second, and so forth. That discovery of October 6, 1995 earned them a Nobel Prize in physics in 2019.

While Dimidium was the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a main sequence star it was not the first exoplanet ever found. See my earlier article on Draugr, Poltergeist, and Phobetor which were discovered in 1992.

This world is about half the mass of Jupiter. That earned it the name Dimidium, meaning half. First estimates put it at .46 Jupiters. Current estimates at the time of this writing put it at 0.61 Jupiters. That four day year makes the planet sit 0.052 AU (Astronomical Units) from its star. 1 AU is the average distance from the Earth to the Sun. So, yeah that’s close. This is a Hot Jupiter.

What the heck is a gas giant doing so close to its star? Gas giants are supposed to be cold, like Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, and Uranus. Indeed Dimidium changed the assumptions of planetary formation. Its peculiar orbit may be due to early gravitational interactions with the protoplanetary disc, causing it to lose energy and spiral inward. There may be a lot of factors at play, like drag, or just the disk-planet dynamics.

We learned that planets do not stay in fixed orbits. That over time they can migrate. Indeed any orbital system with three or more objects is inherently unstable, albeit in solar system configurations over a very long time. Think the three body problem. (Not the books or series, but the phenomenon.) This kind of migration happened in our own solar system, too.

Here’s a great explanation of the positions of Jupiter, Saturn, and why Mars is so small compared to Earth and Venus. https://youtu.be/cPouwOKMS2s?si=yNvWVv4O5D0FGw25

I’ll leave you with a NASA post card from 51 Pegasi b along with my own rendering of this intriguing milestone world and a link to exoplanetary.systems with renderings of all 6300+ exoplanets discovered to date

text:
Phoenix A: a galaxy forming stars at an astonishing rate
r/universe - Phoenix A: a galaxy forming stars at an astonishing rate
The Milky Way forms roughly 1–2 solar masses of new stars per year. But the central galaxy of the Phoenix Cluster has been observed forming stars at roughly 740 solar masses per year. The Phoenix Cluster contains an enormous reservoir of extremely hot gas. As some of that gas loses energy, it cools and becomes denser. Gravity then pulls the cooling gas toward the cluster's center, where it accumulates and eventually condenses into much colder, denser clouds. Inside those clouds, gravity causes pockets of gas and dust to collapse, forming new stars.

It's essentially a chain: Hot gas → cooling → denser gas → molecular clouds → gravitational collapse → new stars

Another major player in the middle is an active supermassive black hole. It is also feeding on the surrounding gas, while its powerful jets inject energy back into the environment and can affect how quickly the gas cools.
